title: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution
summary: Trusted developer utilities proxy execution is the use of legitimate, usually signed, build and debugging tools to run code that the adversary supplies. Because the tool is trusted by the operating system and often already permitted by application control policy, the payload executes inside a process that defenders treat as normal. MSBuild, ClickOnce deployment and the JamPlus build utility are the documented examples, but the pattern extends to any developer tool that compiles, loads or interprets content from a file the attacker can influence. The telemetry shows a trusted binary starting, and the abuse is revealed by context: its parent, its command line, and the path of the file it consumes. Build tooling has no reason to start from a downloads folder, from inside a mail client, or on a workstation that never compiles anything. Detection therefore pairs process creation with file provenance and with the reputation checks the operating system performs before execution.

beginner.definition: Proxy execution means running your own code through somebody else's trusted program. A developer tool is a program used to build, test or debug software. Attackers use these tools because security systems already trust them and allow them to run.
beginner.whyItMatters: Security tools keep lists of programs that are allowed to run. A signed developer tool is usually on that list. If an attacker can make that tool run their code, the security check is bypassed without any exploit. The activity then looks like a normal build step, which is hard to question. This is one reason why an allow list on its own is not enough.
howItWorks: The attacker places a file that the developer tool will read, such as a project or build file.
They start the trusted tool, sometimes from a script, a shortcut or another program.
The tool reads the file and follows its instructions, which include the attacker's code.
The code runs inside the trusted, signed process, so the policy checks were already passed.
The parent process is often unusual, for example a document reader, a mail client or a script host.
The same pattern appears in several different tools, so defenders must look at behaviour rather than one file name.
beginner.example: Imagine a building where the door staff only check badges. A courier with a real company badge walks in every day. If the courier agrees to carry a stranger's parcel inside, the parcel never passes the door check. The badge was real and the courier was allowed to enter. The problem is that nobody looked inside the parcel.
takeaways: Signed and trusted does not mean safe, because the tool can be told what to run.
Look at the parent process and the command line, not only at the tool being started.
Build tools running on ordinary workstations or from download folders deserve a question.

objectives: Explain what proxy execution means and why signed tools are chosen.
Describe how application control can be bypassed without using an exploit.
Identify process lineage evidence that shows a developer tool was abused.
Explain why the provenance of the input file matters more than the tool name.
Describe how the same pattern repeats across several different developer utilities.
